'''''Hymenophyllum tunbrigense''''', the '''Tunbridge filmy fern'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=HYTU2|taxon=Hymenophyllum tunbrigense|accessdate=22 January 2016}}</ref> or '''Tunbridge filmy-fern''',<ref name="BSBI-2007">{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref>  is a small, fragile perennial [[Leptosporangiate fern|leptosporangiate]] [[fern]] which forms large dense colonies of overlapping leaves from creeping rhizomes. The common name derives from the leaves which are very thin, only a single cell thick, and translucent, giving the appearance of a wet film. The evergreen [[fronds]] are [[pinnation|bipinnatifid]], deeply and irregularly dissected, about 3 to 6 cm long, 2 cm across with dark winged [[Stipe (botany)|stipes]]. In contrast to the similar [[Hymenophyllum wilsonii|''H. wilsonii'']] the fronds are more divided, flattened, appressed to the substrate and tend to have a bluish tint.

The fronds are [[monomorphism (biology)|monomorphic]] and produce [[sorus|sori]] along the frond segments close to the [[rachis]].
Up to 5–10 purse-shaped sori are produced per frond, each covered by two strongly convex, flattened [[indusium|indusial]] valves. The valve margins are jagged and used to distinguish ''H. tunbrigense'' from ''[[Hymenophyllum wilsonii|H. wilsonii]]'', where the edges are [[entire leaf|entire]].

In common with all ferns, ''H. tunbrigense'' exhibits a [[gametophyte]] stage in its life cycle ([[alternation of generations]]) and develops a [[haploid]] reproductive [[prothallus]] as an independent plant. Information about the gametophyte is scarce but it is likely to be inconspicuous with a narrow ribbon-like thallus.<ref name="Stokey-1940">Stokey, A.G. (1940). Spore Germination and Vegetative Stages of the Gametophytes of Hymenophyllum and Trichomanes. Bot Gaz 101: 759</ref> The gametophyte may be able to reproduce itself vegetatively by [[Gemma (botany)|gemmae]] in the absence of the sporophyte. Gametophytes of the related Killarney fern (''[[Trichomanes speciosum]]'') have been found outside the geographical range of the sporophyte<ref name="Rumsey-1990">Rumsey, F.J., Sheffield, E., Farrar, D.R (1990) British Filmy-fern gametophytes. Pteridologist 2: pp. 40–42</ref> and this may prove to be true of ''Hymenophyllum tunbrigense''.

==Taxonomy==
The [[basionym]] for the species is ''Trichomanes tunbrigense'', published by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753, based on material from England and Italy. One of the descriptions he cited was that of [[James Petiver]],<ref>{{cite book | title=Species Plantarum |lang=la | volume=II | last=Linnaeus | first=C. | author-link=Carl Linnaeus | year=1753 | publisher=Laurentii Salvii | location=Stockholm |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/359119 |page=1098}}</ref> who collected it near [[Tunbridge Wells]] and described it as ''Darea tunbrigensis minor'', in honor of George Dare who had collected it from the same locality.<ref>{{cite book |last=Petiver |first=James |author-link=James Petiver |title=Musei Petiveriani centuria prima |publisher=S. Smith & B. Walford |location=London |year=1695 |page=[https://archive.org/details/museipetiverian00peti/page/73 73] |url=https://archive.org/details/museipetiverian00peti}}</ref> [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]], in the third volume of ''[[English Botany]]'', transferred it to the genus ''[[Hymenophyllum]]'' in 1794, based on the two-[[valve (botany)|valve]]d indusium (rather than the tubular indusium of ''Trichomanes'' ''sensu stricto'').<ref>{{cite book |last=Smith |first=James Edward |author-link=James Edward Smith (botanist) |others=illustrated by James Sowerby |title=English Botany |volume=3 |year=1794 |publisher=J. Davis |location=London |page=162 |url=http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/ing/Libro.php?Libro=2038&Pagina=49 |access-date=2016-10-08 |archive-date=2016-10-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009172917/http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/ing/Libro.php?Libro=2038&Pagina=49 }}</ref> <!-- other synonyms -->

==Distribution==

Apparently worldwide, but discontinuous, in distribution but most frequent in western European [[ocean]]ic regions like the British Isles. There is uncertainty whether similar plants found in Mexico, the West Indies, Central America, South America, South Africa and Asia should also be included in this species.
''H. tunbrigense'' has a similar though distinct distribution to ''[[Hymenophyllum wilsonii|H. wilsonii]]'' and can also be found in North America. Its habitat preference may mean that it has been under-recorded in many less-well populated parts of the world.

In continental Europe it occurs much further east than ''[[Hymenophyllum wilsonii|H. wilsonii]]'' but these sites are very [[disjunct distribution|disjunct]] and may represent [[Relict (biology)|relict]] populations from a different climatic period. Many of the continental populations are declining or have disappeared in recent times.

The specific name is derived from [[Royal Tunbridge Wells]] in [[Kent]], England which was one of its disjunct eastern localities in Britain.

==Ecology and conservation==

Filmy ferns (''[[Hymenophyllum]]'' species, ''[[Trichomanes]]'' species) are very vulnerable to desiccation which limits the habitats in which they can survive. ''[[Hymenophyllum]]'' species are dependent as much, or more, upon the [[microclimate]] of a site as the [[macroclimate]]. ''H. tunbrigense'' is usually associated with rock outcrops, especially when deep fissures or crevices are present.

''Hymenophyllum tunbrigense'' appears not to reproduce effectively from spores under present environmental conditions. Gametophytes have not been identified in the field although there is circumstantial evidence that sexual reproduction does take place.<ref name="Richards-1972">Richards, P.W., Evans, G.B. (1972). Biological Flora of the British Isles. No. 126. Hymenophyllum tunbrigense (L.) Sm. (pp. 245–258), Hymenophyllum wilsonii Hooker (258–268). Journal of Ecology 60.</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
While there are records of its cultivation ([[Harold Stuart Thompson]] grew a specimen from Somerset in a bell jar in his bedroom for a decade),<ref>H.S. Thompson ''s.n.'', August 1886, http://herbariaunited.org/specimen/259752/</ref> it is not generally cultivated. It is propagated at [[Kew Gardens]] for reestablishment in suitable habitat.<ref>{{cite web | title=Hymenophyllum tunbrigense (Tunbridge filmy fern) |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew | url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30002980-2 | access-date=8 October 2016}}</ref>
